catalog_quote: Tonal systems are consistently absent in the Torricelli languages (relevant here are the One varieties), and the western languages (Sentani, Tobati, Ningera). The tonal systems in the phonologies of the Skou family languages are completely dominant, and remarkably comparable (Donohue 2003). Tonality in the Serra Hills languages varies inversely with their distance from the Skou languages, suggesting that tone is an areal phenomenon supported by the simple syllable-based tone systems of the Skou languages. The tonal system of Barupu is complex (Crowther 2000), but shows simplification in terms of the accentual features, influence perhaps from the Sissano Lagoon area. [p.182, Table 4: Comparative suprasegmental inventories; columns Pitches / Nasalisation / Sissano Lagoon area?; rows:] Serra Hills ... Womo H L I ... Sumararu H L F R I || Donohue 2004:65: Skou is related distantly to the languages of the Serra Hills and Piore River families. While no detailed phonological work has been carried out on the Serra Hills languages, it is known that they possess tone systems with up to five or even six contrastive pitches on monosyllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Womo is recorded (from Donohue's own 2000 survey wordlists) as a tone language with at least contrastive High and Low pitches (fewer pitch contrasts than its Serra Hills sisters Sumararu, Rawo, Puare with H L F R); the sources say nothing about word stress or accent placement in Womo, and Donohue states explicitly that no detailed phonological work exists for the Serra Hills languages.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The F and R pitch cells for Womo are shaded in Table 4 (contour pitches undetermined/uncertain). For the closest analysed relative, Puare, Donohue 2004:67-68 describes five word-level tone melodies plus a contrastive accent located within the final two syllables of the phonological word; no such analysis is given for Womo.
new_statements.domain_note: Survey-level inventory tables built from elicited citation-form wordlists (Donohue's 2000 walking survey Vanimo-Aitape; per-word pitch letters in Donohue 2004 Appendix 5). No word- vs phrase-level analysis for Womo.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe 'Womo' = the language of Onei village (ISO wmx; Miller 2016 calls it 'Pin'), from Donohue's 2000 survey. Glottolog womo1238 'Womo-Sumararu' lumps Womo with Sumararu, which Donohue treats as a separate Serra Hills language and lists separately in the same tables (Sumararu: pitches H L F R + I; vowels incl. a front rounded y). The tone statement in Donohue 2004:65 is at the level of the Serra Hills group (Puare, Rawo, Sumararu, Womo, Mori), not Womo individually.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura & Matthew S. Dryer. 2021. The tone system of Poko-Rawo (Skou). Phonological Data and Analysis 3(1): 1-32. Linguistic Society of America / Cambridge Core.
tone_statements.quote: Other members of the family include I’saka (Donohue and San Roque 2004), Wutung (Marmion 2010), Skou (Donohue 2003), Barapu/Warapu (Corris 2006), Puare, Vanimo/Dumo (Ross 1980), Womo/Onei, and Sumararu.1 To the best of our knowledge (though many Skou languages remain underdocumented), all members of the family are tonal. [...] Poko belongs to a different branch of the Skou family than any of the tone systems described; the other languages in its branch are virtually undocumented. We have gathered very preliminary data for its closer relative spoken in Sumararu, and the surface pitch patterns are reminiscent of Poko. It could be that the switch to a three-tone system occurred at the time this branch split from the others, but more data are required to evaluate this hypothesis.
